title: 3  Three Readers, One Record
text:
At three o’clock on a rainy Tuesday afternoon, three people are looking at the exact same line of data on their screens. In our provincial laboratory in Vietnam, a technician named Vy stares at a row of text showing forty-eight polymerase chain reaction cycles completed at midnight. For her, this line is her only shield, the physical proof of her ten-hour night shift. Down the hall, her supervisor looks at the same line because a query about a contaminated batch just arrived. For him, this row of text is a liability map, a way to find who is answerable for the error. Thousands of miles away in an air-conditioned office, a program officer opens a database. He has never seen our cramped room, but he paid for the reagents. For him, this line is a consumption metric, proof that the materials did not expire in a warehouse. All three are reading the same entry at the same moment. Yet, they see three entirely different realities.
Our data served the institution, the funder and the auditor. It did not serve the person who produced it, and nobody designed it that way on purpose. Modern laboratory informatics has built sophisticated tracking systems that view attribution purely as an instrument of blame and auditing. In Vietnam, thirty-eight laboratories have implemented open-source LIMS with US CDC support. However, these systems are managed provincially and lack individual, machine-enforced audit trails. When something goes wrong, we search the logs to find who to punish. When something goes right, the technician’s labor remains completely invisible.
Our proposal is to turn this shared line of data into a voluntary point-accumulation asset owned by the worker. Rather than using it as a top-down surveillance tool, the technician can export her own verified contributions as a portable professional credential. This shift from surveillance to self-owned progress is supported by strong behavioral science. Meta-analyses on Perceived Organizational Support show that development opportunities are among the strongest drivers of employee commitment.
It is necessary to design this registry carefully to avoid the traps of gamification. For instance, studies on status tiers show that demoting an individual damages loyalty, so our system will never demote a user. We also reject daily streaks and point expiration, which behavioral literature shows can lead to data gaming or burnout. Instead, we rely on established concepts like endowed progress, where providing an initial, justified jumpstart on a progress record has been shown to increase completion rates from nineteen to thirty-four percent in field experiments.
However, we must remain completely honest about our limits. While behavioral mechanisms like endowed progress and goal gradients are well-documented in marketing studies, their application to healthcare is mostly untested. There is currently absolutely no trial evidence or randomized controlled studies evaluating how a worker-owned, point-accumulation registry affects reporting accuracy or staff retention in low-resource public health laboratories. We are proposing a logical, evidence-informed pilot of twelve months to test these ideas. By connecting the machine’s serial number to a technician’s name, we can satisfy the supervisor’s need for accountability, the funder’s need for tracking, and the worker’s need for visible, portable credit.
Many digital systems and data initiatives come and go. Most of them arrived with a great deal of noise, only to end up abandoned. They died because of a fundamental flaw in their architecture. They were built for only one party. In the world of public health, if you design a system that serves only a single group, you are writing its death sentence.
Most of the tools we were forced to use were built entirely for the funder. The international donors or the high-level administrators wanted clean reports and compliance metrics. Because the system was designed only for their eyes, we on the laboratory floor felt policed and monitored. We saw the software as an intrusive eye that tracked our minutes without offering us any value. When staff feel watched, they naturally resist. They find ways to work around the system, or worse, they begin to fabricate numbers just to make the charts look green. The data becomes a performance, and the system dies of its own falsehood.
Conversely, you can try to build a system solely for the worker. You can design an app that helps us track our daily tasks or manage our own professional learning. But if the system serves only the worker, it hits a different wall. Nobody wants to pay to run it. Government agencies and international donors will not fund a platform that does not provide them with verified, actionable data. Without their financial support, the technology cannot survive, and the project quickly collapses once the initial enthusiasm fades.
The proposal does not choose between those readers. It rests on one observation: the same record can serve all three of them at once.
For the worker, the record is a self-owned portfolio of verified labor. It is their personal point-accumulation ledger that they can carry with them to unlock professional opportunities, like scholarships. For the funder, this very same record is trusted, tamper-evident proof of activity. They can see that the tests were actually run, satisfying their need for accountability without forcing us to feel policed. For the institution, the third reader, the same record answers the question of who did what on which day, which is the question its own regulator will eventually ask it. Further downstream sits a fourth party who is not one of the three but matters to all of them: the educational partner or licensing body, which can read a record it did not have to trust on faith. That reader is the reason the record has to be portable rather than merely tidy.



One record, three readers. The same row of data, read by three parties who currently want different things from it. Nothing new is collected; only who may read it changes.


We should be entirely honest about the limits of this design. A tamper-proof log of fabricated entries is still just a tamper-proof lie, and cryptography does nothing about what a person types in the first place. I made a claim in an earlier draft that I have since decided is wrong: that aligning the three readers around one record removes the incentive to cheat. It does the opposite. So long as the log was only an institutional liability record, a technician had little to gain from inventing runs. The moment those lines convert into scholarship tiers and portable credentials, every entry becomes personally valuable, and the incentive to inflate counts, log runs that never happened, or work under a colleague’s login rises accordingly. Making the record worth something necessarily makes it worth faking. Supervisor co-signature and spot-audit are the controls we have, and both are vulnerable in exactly the setting this proposal targets, where the supervisor countersigning may be the same person whose unit is measured by the total. Any honest pilot has to treat verification fraud as a live failure mode to be measured, not a risk that good design has already dissolved. We transform a tool of surveillance into a mutual asset.
Our staff work under a system that makes their daily labor invisible. When we write logs or enter data, we are creating records that could serve multiple purposes. Yet, most systems fail because they are built to be read by only one party. In this proposal, I want to describe a system designed for three readers at once, using a single digital record.
The first reader of this record is the worker. Today, if a technician spends five years running thousands of PCR tests in a provincial lab, they leave with nothing but a blank paper resume. They have no portable proof of their work. I am proposing a self-owned digital portfolio that is a permanent, verified record of their actual labour. It is a record that says, for example, I performed four thousand two hundred verified diagnostic tests over these specific years under a unique digital signature. This is not a symbolic badge or a superficial points system. It is a portable professional asset. It belongs entirely to the worker, and they can carry it with them when they move between different employers or apply for advanced training.
The second reader of this record is the institution. In our current provincial labs, there is often deep confusion about who did what on any given day. To solve this, our proposal borrows the strict data integrity standards of the international pharmaceutical industry, specifically the ALCOA framework. In these standards, the very first letter stands for Attributable. This means a record must show exactly who performed a test and when they did it, mapped against a unique digital identity. When an institution reads our proposed database, they gain absolute clarity about individual responsibility. They can see exactly who processed each tube, who ran each assay, and who verified the results.
However, we must be completely honest about the limits of this design and preserve some important caveats. The ALCOA standard was originally created for highly regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing and clinical trial laboratories. None of these regulations were written for a provincial preventive medicine laboratory in Vietnam. Applying them here is a deliberate borrowing of high-status industry practices, not a legal requirement. Furthermore, in the existing industry frameworks, attribution is treated almost entirely as a mechanism of blame and auditing. It is designed to find out who to blame when a record is wrong or when a test fails. Shared logins are a classic inspection finding because they destroy this accountability. The breakthrough of our design is that we do not use attribution to police or blame our staff. Instead, we transform this institutional record of responsibility into a positive, portable professional credit owned by the worker. We make the same record serve both the technician and the institution without adding administrative weight.
In those years, I handled thousands of diagnostic test kits bought with international donor money. I saw how much effort went into tracking these resources. Yet, as I write this proposal, I must point out a massive gap in how we account for these materials. This brings us to the third reader of our proposed record: the funder. Under our design, the donor finally gains the ability to see exactly when a reagent bought with its money was used, by whom it was used, and for what specific test.
To understand why this is a breakthrough, we must look at how donor commodities are tracked today. The global health system relies on major supply chain programmes and software platforms like OpenLMIS. These systems are supported by organizations like Gavi and the Global Fund. But if you look closely at these tools, they only trace commodities as far as the physical facility. They show that a box of reagents arrived at a provincial warehouse or was delivered to a specific clinic. After that, the trace goes completely cold. The systems can only record aggregate consumption. They cannot link a specific vial of chemical reagent to an individual diagnostic test. They cannot tell you which named operator actually ran the test, or on which day, or for which patient. (1,2)
Some people argue that modern instrument connectivity solves this problem. Many laboratories use middleware to connect high-throughput machines, such as viral load analyzers, directly to database systems. But this connectivity does not solve the human accountability gap. It attributes activity to a physical machine rather than a named person. The system logs that the analyzer ran fifty tests, but it does not tell you who prepared the samples, who calibrated the instrument, or who was responsible for the run.



Where the trace goes cold. Current tracking terminates at the clinic door and the machine casing. The proposal extends the same trace by one more step, to the person who ran the test.


It is worth being exact about what exists today and what does not. There is currently no open-source laboratory information management system in low and middle-income countries that features cryptographic immutability by default. No international donor currently requires tracing chemical reagents down to individual operators. Implementing this level of traceability is our own deliberate design choice, not a legal mandate or a donor requirement. The limits of input honesty set out earlier apply here in full: the chain protects a record after it is written, and nothing more.
By closing this gap, we transform how donors view their investments. Instead of just seeing shipments arrive at a building, they see their funding actively turn into verified human labor on the laboratory floor.
Much hard work goes completely unrecorded. The most significant gap in our entire global health data architecture. When you look at how laboratory data is managed today, every single existing framework treats attribution as a mechanism for blame and auditing. In these regulatory structures, knowing who performed an action is only useful when something goes wrong. If a data entry is incorrect, or if an assay fails, the system is used to identify the person responsible. It is a tool for policing and finding fault. Shared logins are treated as major inspection findings because they break this chain of blame. Yet, this focus on fault-finding wastes something.
Currently, no regulator, no laboratory information system, no logistics platform, and no international donor has turned this very same record into positive, portable credit owned by the person who performed the work. If a technician runs four thousand tests over three years with absolute precision, that achievement is completely lost to history. The system logs their name for auditing, but they leave their job with a blank paper resume. There is absolutely no established standard for exporting a verified service history as a professional asset. Under the current system, a worker’s hard labor is treated as an institutional commodity rather than their own professional property. We have built elaborate, expensive structures to trace reagents and monitor machinery, but we have completely failed to build a mechanism that allows workers to own the proof of their own competence.
It is worth being plain about the existing tools and their limitations. Some administrative platforms, such as iHRIS or the Workload Indicators of Staffing Need tool, are designed to track staffing numbers, training levels, and overall workload estimates. However, these systems remain completely disconnected from actual daily laboratory logs. Other modern security frameworks, such as blockchain protocols for auditing electronic health records, are designed to log who accessed or edited files. Yet, their focus is entirely on data security and detecting abuse. They were never intended to record positive professional achievements or provide portable career credits. Furthermore, we must acknowledge a vital caveat. No open-source laboratory database in low and middle-income countries currently features cryptographic immutability by default, and no international donor requires tracing work down to individual operators. Implementing this in our local clinics is a choice, not a legal requirement. By transforming the institutional audit trail into a verified service record, we can allow workers to own their professional history. This turns a tool of surveillance into a ladder of opportunity, helping the unconnected prove their worth.
When we talk about global health, we often speak in terms of charity or moral obligation. There is a version of this argument addressed to funders instead, and I will put it plainly rather than at length. Programmes that support laboratory capacity abroad do so on the reasoning that detection is cheaper and earlier at the source. That reasoning depends on the people at the source still being there next year.
This is the honest reading of what our proposed system is and what it is not. I must state a vital caveat from the outset. This recognition pathway is not an early warning system itself. It will not automatically detect a new pathogen or trigger an emergency alert. Instead, it is the quiet machinery that keeps the workforce operating the early warning system from falling apart. By transforming invisible daily sweat into a verified professional asset, we ensure that trained technicians stay in their jobs longer and produce more timely, reliable diagnostic data. We are securing the human foundation of health security. Without stable, motivated people on the laboratory floor, even the most expensive surveillance machinery is useless.
The cost of failing to stop health threats at their source is staggering. To understand the scale of this risk, we can look at the economic impact of the last major global crisis. According to a 2020 paper by Cutler and Summers published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, COVID-19 cost the United States roughly 16 trillion dollars. This is an almost unimaginable sum of money. However, we must preserve the strict honesty caveats attached to this figure. First, the text notes that about half of that 16 trillion dollar estimate represents non-market health loss, such as the value of lost lives and mental health impacts, rather than direct lost economic output. Second, we must acknowledge that this paper is a short viewpoint article rather than a peer-reviewed, complex economic modeling study. It is a simplified estimate, not a definitive final calculation (3,4).
Yet, even with these necessary caveats, the message is undeniable. The economic and human cost of a delayed response dwarfs any local investment in public health systems. When a provincial laboratory in a place like Vietnam cannot retain its staff, the delay in detecting a novel threat can ripple across oceans in days. By investing in a digital pathway that verifies and honors the work of frontline technicians, the United States keeps the people who operate that capacity in place. Equipment is the part that gets counted. The person who runs it at two in the morning is the part that walks away, and replacing her costs more than keeping her.
During that time, I watched valuable investments quietly decay. When we talk about global health security, we often look at the staggering scale of the financial numbers involved. If we look at the cost of global pandemic preparedness, the figures presented by major international health bodies are massive. The G20 High Level Independent Panel, in its July 2021 report, estimated that global pandemic preparedness requires roughly 15 billion dollars a year in additional international funding. Just a few months later, in March 2022, the World Health Organization and the World Bank presented a report to the G20 estimating the total preparedness need at 31.1 billion dollars a year, with 10.5 billion of that representing additional international funding. On these numbers, the record deserves a plain statement. They are not bottom-up cost calculations with precise confidence intervals. Instead, they are expert consensus estimates designed primarily for policy advocacy (3–5).
Some advocates justify these investments by quoting dramatic return-on-investment multiples. The trouble is that the published multiples do not agree with one another; they differ by orders of magnitude depending on which costs are counted and over what horizon. In this proposal, I deliberately refuse to quote any specific return multiple. I do this because those multiples are simple ratios rather than counterfactual models. They do not survive strict economic scrutiny and fail to account for complex real-world variables.
However, the core of my argument does not rely on these grand global estimates. There is a deep cost asymmetry at play here. While the world debates tens of billions of dollars, the local reality on the laboratory floor is far more modest. This proposal does not ask for a single dollar of new, unallocated money. It does not ask for a new budget line from any donor or ministry. Instead, the real argument is that this proposal asks that what has already been invested does not decay (3,4).
In Vietnam, the marginal dollar should not be used to build new facilities or buy more high-throughput machinery. We already have a preventive health network that reaches every province and extends down to the commune level, though as of June 2025 there are thirty four provinces where there were sixty three, and the network is still settling into that new shape (6). The legal rails are already in place through Circular Thirty-Two, which mandates continuous medical education hours. Even the US CDC has already invested in deploying open-source laboratory information systems across thirty-eight local laboratories. They have also supported quality management systems to help ten laboratories achieve ISO accreditation. The infrastructure is there, but without a stable, motivated workforce, it is slowly falling apart as trained technicians leave for the private sector. This proposal is incredibly cheap because it does not require us to construct something from nothing. It merely asks to connect the existing pieces that are already paid for, so that earlier investments keep working. It is a small, controlled option on a massive potential payoff.
During those years of processing diagnostic samples, I often thought about where these threats actually originate. In this proposal, I want to write about where new diseases actually come from, and I want to do so carefully, without pointing fingers or placing blame on local cultures. When a new virus emerges, it is not a moral failing of a specific community. The real scientific drivers of emerging infectious diseases are ecological and physical. They are driven by rapid land use change, rising livestock density, and the expanding human-animal interface.
The data on this is very clear. In a landmark 2008 study published in Nature, Kate Jones and her colleagues analyzed three hundred and thirty-five emerging infectious disease events. They found that sixty point three percent of these emerging infectious disease events are zoonotic, meaning they jump from animals to humans. Furthermore, seventy-one point eight percent of those zoonotic events originate specifically in wildlife. A later study in 2017 by Allen mapped these hotspots globally. His team showed that these hotspots are heavily correlated with land use change, mammal diversity, and human population density. Southeast Asia, including Vietnam, frequently appears on these maps. This is not because of cultural habits or local eating practices. It is because our region has a high diversity of mammals, particularly bats, combined with rapid forest fragmentation and dense human and livestock populations (7–9).
But we must look at the structural forces behind these ecological pressures. It is necessary to be honest about the fact that forest fragmentation and agricultural expansion in developing nations are substantially driven by global economic demand for commodities. Additionally, we must state a critical scientific caveat regarding these hotspot maps. Hotspot maps are partly an artifact of surveillance effort. Countries that spend more money looking for viruses and reporting them will naturally show up as hotspots, whereas regions with minimal surveillance remain blank. The map reflects where we look, not just where the viruses are.
This is why Vietnam’s position matters. We are a frontline partner and a gatekeeper in global health security. We stand at the precise interface where these ecological pressures collide. This is where the modest claim made earlier has to be repeated rather than escalated: the pathway does not detect anything. It keeps the people who operate the detection in place. The marginal dollar spent here by international partners should not be used for building new clinics or buying redundant equipment. We do not need more concrete. Instead, the marginal dollar must be spent on activating what already exists, connecting the legal rails and local infrastructure we have already paid for.
There is a standard objection at this point: that aid only works where institutions are already strong, so weak systems should be built before they are funded. That claim came from Burnside and Dollar, and it did not survive replication; Easterly, Levine and Roodman showed in 2004 that the interaction disappears once the dataset is extended. The related folk history, that Germany and Japan recovered because their institutions outlived their factories, is also not what economic historians find. I raise these only to set them aside, because neither the objection nor its rebuttal decides anything here (10).
Therefore, institutional capacity does not determine whether money should flow. It determines the channel through which money works. In Vietnam, our marginal dollar does not need to build new capacity from scratch. We do not need a massive, expensive overhaul. The preventive medicine network is already established in every province down to the communes, Circular thirty-two already provides our legal continuing medical education rails, and the US CDC has already placed open-source laboratory information management systems in thirty-eight labs. Our proposal is incredibly cheap because it does not demand new capacity. It simply connects what already exists.
In writing this proposal, I want to discuss the official rationale of global health security and the honest limits of the statistics we use to support it. The overarching framework of our field is organized around the Global Health Security Agenda, which has used the prevent, detect, and respond triad since 2014. The United States published a Global Health Security Strategy in April 2024 that reinforced this framing. That strategy has since been withdrawn and was replaced in September 2025 by the America First Global Health Strategy, which moves to multi-year bilateral agreements meant to end what the State Department calls a prolonged period of dependency. I mention the change because a proposal that cites a withdrawn strategy as current policy deserves to be read with suspicion, and because the newer framing makes this argument easier rather than harder. Read the commitments in it. Those agreements are to guarantee that frontline healthcare workers keep being funded for the term, and the department undertakes to work with each country to ensure there are data systems in place. Frontline workers and the systems that record them are named in the same paragraph of current American policy. What is missing is the join between them. A record that stays with the worker is exactly what survives a transition to self-reliance. Officially, the United States CDC’s Division of Global Health Protection reports an impressive role in supporting the containment of over two hundred and fifty outbreaks in the year 2024 alone. This is the grand narrative that justifies international intervention. (11–13)
However, when we look at the specific performance targets on the ground, the numbers become much more normative than experimental. Consider the widely cited seven-one-seven target, which calls for detecting an outbreak within seven days, notifying public health authorities within one day, and completing an early response within seven days. This formula is useful, but we must state clearly that it is a normative target chosen for memorability rather than a precise threshold derived from scientific experiments. When we examine actual implementation data published in 2023 across forty-one health events in countries like Brazil, Ethiopia, Liberia, Nigeria, and Uganda, the reality is sobering. While fifty-four percent of events met the detection target and seventy-one percent met the notification target, only forty-nine percent met the early response target. In fact, only about twenty-seven percent, or roughly a quarter of all assessed events, met all three targets. (5,13)
The same pattern shows in those financing estimates I quoted earlier. They are expert consensus shaped by policy advocacy, not bottom-up costings with confidence intervals around them. That does not make them worthless; it makes them political indicators rather than blueprints, and a proposal that leans on them should say which of the two it is relying on. (3–5)
Our proposal is not trying to resolve these global macroeconomic debates. We are proposing a highly contained, local pilot of a verified service record for our technicians. By running a single staff position on our existing legal continuing medical education rails, we can test these behavioral models cheaply. If we want to achieve targets like seven-one-seven, we must first make the daily, invisible labor of our local laboratory technicians visible.

title: 4  From Record to Door
text:
In London a surgical trainee opens his intercollegiate e-logbook and enters a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. His supervisor countersigns it the same day. Three years of hernia repairs, appendix removals and assisted incisions sit in that file, each one dated, each one signed by somebody other than him. At national selection the panel does not ask him to describe his experience. It reads the count.
At the same hour in a provincial CDC in Vietnam, a laboratory technician finishes her ten-thousandth polymerase chain reaction assay. She has been at the bench since the previous evening. When she logs off, the count goes nowhere. There is no file with her name on it, no countersignature, nothing a committee could read. Her five years exist in shift rosters and internal reports that were never built to leave the building, and in the memory of a supervisor who will retire.
Two people, the same trade in the sense that both are trusted with a patient’s diagnosis, the same hour of the same day. One of them has a record. That is the whole of the difference, and it is not a difference in skill.
During those long shifts of processing diagnostic assays, I watched how the absolute invisibility of our field work limits our professional lives. When we propose a digital registry to record the verified contributions of our technicians, we must look at the real-world models that actually work. The British surgical logbook, the flight logs of the Federal Aviation Administration, and the portfolios of the National Board for Professional Teaching Standards in the United States all share the same structural engine. They succeed because they meet three rigid conditions. First, the record is verified by an external supervisor. Second, the record is tied directly to a real career gateway held by an authority. Third, the reward is substantial, such as a specialized training slot or a salary upgrade, rather than a symbolic badge.
The weakest link is worth naming first. Our technology can easily handle the verification of these records. However, the system only works if we can secure a real educational partner to hold open the career gateways. We are proposing tiered scholarships of twenty-five, fifty, and seventy-five percent for our certified technicians rather than symbolic micro-credentials. I should state the evidence position on badges once, carefully, because it is easy to overstate and I have overstated it in earlier drafts. I am not aware of independent peer-reviewed evidence that a digital badge, on its own, raises promotion or retention; most of the effectiveness material I could find comes from the platforms that issue and sell them. That is an absence of evidence in the sources available to me, which is not the same as proof that badges do nothing, and I would revise this paragraph if a reader pointed me to a trial I have missed. What follows from it is modest: do not build the pathway on the badge. Build it on the gate the badge is supposed to open.
Our daily work vanishes into thin air. We ran thousands of critical assays, but when we went home, we had nothing to show for it. In this proposal, I am suggesting that we build a verified portfolio of labor. To some, this might sound like a theoretical experiment, but we do not need to invent this concept from scratch. We can look directly at three concrete, highly successful models that already run on this exact architecture.
The first model is British. Surgical trainees in the United Kingdom do not apply with reference letters describing their promise. They submit the summary sheet of a consolidation report from the Intercollegiate Surgical eLogbook, and the NHS guidance is unusually specific about what it will accept. The sheet shows the number of procedures and the date range. Cases assisted or supervised count; cases merely observed do not. Every page must be signed by a consultant giving their full name, their General Medical Council number and the date, and that consultant may ask to see the whole logbook before signing. The resulting count is then banded: forty cases or more scores an A, thirty to thirty-nine a B, twenty to twenty-nine a C, eleven to nineteen a D, ten or fewer an E. (1)
That system settles several things before anyone argues about them. It defines what counts as taking part. It requires an attester who is himself identified by a registration number, so the countersignature can be traced to a person who can be asked about it. And it converts a count into a band, so two candidates can be compared without anyone writing a paragraph about character. None of this is novel and none of it is expensive. It is simply decided, and written down, and applied the same way to everybody.
The second model is found in aviation. After the Colgan Air crash in 2009, Congress directed the Federal Aviation Administration to raise the experience required of airline pilots. The rule that resulted, 14 CFR 61.159, sets an airline transport pilot certificate at fifteen hundred hours of logged flight time, and 14 CFR 121.436 is what obliges the airline to hire only pilots who hold it. A logbook is not a resume builder in that system. It is the legal gate. (2)
What matters more for this proposal is the part of the rule that is usually left out of the summary. The fifteen hundred hours are not absolute. A pilot who graduated from an approved four-year aviation degree can hold a restricted certificate at one thousand hours; a two-year degree brings it to twelve hundred and fifty; a military pilot to seven hundred and fifty. The regulator did not lower its standard for those pilots. It accepted a different, verified record in place of raw hours. That is exactly the shape of what I am proposing, and it already exists in American federal law, in a safety system with no appetite for sentiment. A verified record of structured work can substitute for a cruder count, provided somebody outside the applicant certifies it. (1–3)
The third model belongs to education. American teachers can seek National Board Certification, and they do not do it by sitting an exam. They assemble a portfolio: video of their own classrooms, work their students actually produced, and written analysis of both. Twenty-nine states then attach money to the result. Washington pays 6,514 dollars a year, with up to another 5,000 for teachers in qualifying high-poverty schools. Hawaii pays 5,000 and doubles it for high-need schools. Delaware pays twelve percent of base salary. Idaho and South Dakota pay 2,000. (3)
Two things are worth taking from that spread. The first is that the money is real enough to change a household budget, which is what separates this from a badge. The second is that it is not guaranteed: in March 2025 Washington was reported to be considering cutting the bonus for thousands of its certified teachers. Even the strongest example of a record converting into money is a political decision that can be revisited, and a proposal that pretends otherwise is not being straight with anyone. (3)
These three diverse fields prove that a self-recorded log can become a powerful professional asset. They also agree on what makes one work, and the three conditions they share are worth taking one at a time.
The weakest link in this proposal is the gate. A verified ledger of laboratory work is worth little unless somebody on the other side of a door agrees to read it. If nobody does, we are handing our staff symbolic digital badges.
I should be careful here, because in an earlier draft I wrote that a single educational partner was the whole prerequisite, and then spent several pages describing American certification routes and graduate admissions as though they were separate benefits. Both cannot be true. What is true is that there is more than one gate, and they are not equally likely. The nearest and most realistic is domestic: a provincial or national training institution, a promotion panel, a transfer decision, a place on a course. Further out, and for a small minority, sit the international routes described later in this chapter, which are real but narrow and slow. The proposal needs at least one gate open to be worth building, and it should be judged on the domestic one, since that is where almost every technician this book is about will actually stand. The evidence position on badges stated earlier applies here. I have to secure a real gatekeeper to make this work.
The first condition is that the record of labor must be verified by someone outside of the worker. A self-declared logbook holds no weight on its own. In a laboratory setting, a technician cannot simply write down that they ran a test and expect others to believe it. There must be an independent verifier, such as a laboratory supervisor, who confirms the entry using a unique digital signature. Without this external verification, the database is nothing more than a list of unproven claims.
The second condition is that the log must be tied to a real door that someone already controls. In the UK surgical model, that door is a national selection panel for training. In American aviation, it is the legal gate to an airline first officer seat. For teachers in the United States, a complex portfolio of classroom video and student work converts directly into a substantial annual stipend. If we build a system of records without a corresponding gatekeeper who holds the keys to real career advancement, we are wasting our time. The record must lead directly to a specific, tangible opportunity that already exists in the administrative framework.
The third condition is that the reward must be substantive. By substantive, we mean actual training opportunities, professional licensing, or direct financial compensation, such as an annual stipend. We should not be offering our workers symbolic tokens or digital badges. The honest position on this point, caveat included, is this. This is the same limit noted above. Every single claim of their effectiveness traces back to the marketing materials of the platforms that sell and issue these badges. There is no trial data supporting their value on their own.
Our proposal is built on these three pillars. It is an honest design that avoids the trap of empty gamification. Underpaid staff deserve better than a sticker. Instead, we want to build a verified record that connects directly to the existing legal rails of continuous medical education and real training slots. By respecting these three strict conditions, we can turn a simple laboratory log into a genuine professional asset that our workers can carry with them to build their futures.
I know how easy it is to make a paper log look perfect. But when we talk about creating digital, immutable records of laboratory labor, we have to face a hard truth. A tamper-proof log of fabricated entries is still only a tamper-proof lie. Cryptography can prevent anyone from changing a record after it is saved, but it cannot stop a technician from entering fake data at the start. To solve this hardest of problems, we must build an objective verification layer. That layer is external quality assessment, commonly known as EQA.
Under EQA, the laboratory is sent blind proficiency panels without any warning. Because these samples arrive randomly and are prepared by an external party, they cannot be self-reported, anticipated, or gamed. The technician must process them exactly like regular samples. EQA is not a speculative or experimental concept. It is globally recognized as the gold standard for laboratory quality. Participation in EQA is strictly mandatory under international standards like ISO 15189, which requires labs to join inter-laboratory comparison programs and document corrective actions when results drift. In the United States, passing proficiency testing under the CLIA rules is a mandatory condition of laboratory certification (4–6).
Vietnam is not starting from scratch here. We have a solid legal framework for this. Under Decision 2429 of 2017, issued by the Ministry of Health, laboratories are evaluated using a national quality criteria set. Our designated national quality control centres manage these schemes and publish national proficiency testing data. Furthermore, we have shown that we can push this high level of quality control deep into the field. The National Institute of Hygiene and Epidemiology and the Pasteur Institute have successfully taken external quality assessment down to the commune level for HIV testing. We have proven that even remote, rural health staff can participate in rigorous quality control networks (5,7,8).
However, we must be completely honest about the limits of these existing programs. Every EQA scheme running today is designed to assess the laboratory as a whole institution, not the individual worker. Currently, there is absolutely no published data on individual-level EQA performance for provincial CDC technicians in Vietnam. Suggesting that we already evaluate individual personnel through EQA here would be mere speculation. Furthermore, there is a real risk of purpose drift. Historically, under CLIA, laboratories have been caught giving special treatment to proficiency samples because the stakes were too high. When you turn EQA into a high-stakes test of an individual, you create a blame culture that forces people to hide errors rather than report them. To avoid this trap, our proposal does not record whether an individual passed or failed a panel. Instead, we log that a technician has successfully participated in a set number of external quality rounds under a rotation mechanism, alongside their documented corrective actions when discrepancies occurred. This is meant to record professional discipline without turning quality assessment into a game of fear, but I do not want to claim it escapes the problem it is designed around. It relocates the problem. If a logged corrective action feeds a scholarship tier, then a discrepancy becomes something a technician and their supervisor both have reason to bury, or to paper over with a corrective action written for the file rather than for the bench. The incentive lands on the same pair of people who already sign off on everything else.
There is also a volume problem worth conceding. An external quality panel arrives a few times a year. It cannot testify to the thousands of routine assays described at the start of this book; it can only testify that when the laboratory was tested blind, it performed. Those are different claims. External assessment is what makes the record credible to an outside reader, and routine volume is what makes it substantial to the worker who built it. Neither one substitutes for the other, and a pilot that measures only the first will not know whether the second is honest. No system in the world has yet turned EQA participation into a portable individual credential, but by doing so, we can finally verify the worker’s true competence.
Our staff struggle to prove their daily labor. In this proposal, I want to address a critical design correction regarding how we verify laboratory labor through external quality assessment, or EQA. Standard practice in global health always scores the laboratory as a whole institution, not the individual person. If you look at standard laboratory audits, this institutional focus seems absolute. However, there are some narrow, existing precedents for individual tracking that we must examine. Under the American CLIA rules, proficiency testing samples must be handled by the routine staff who actually perform the testing, and these samples must be rotated among them. This rotation means the specific individual running the sample is already documented in the laboratory’s records, and this proficiency testing can serve as a valid input for annual personnel competency assessments. Furthermore, the British NHS cervical screening programme goes even further and actively assesses individual staff competence, covering around one thousand one hundred and nineteen personnel across sixty-three laboratories twice a year, while schemes like UK NEQAS Digital Morphology also accept individual registrations.
Therefore, our proposed system makes a vital design correction. The digital ledger will never show a personal pass or fail score for an individual technician. Instead, the database will document two things only. It will show a technician’s active participation across official sample rotations. It will also record their documented corrective action when a result was out of consensus with the reference group. Logging how a technician handles a discrepancy shows true professional discipline and honesty. It proves they can participate in a rigorous quality loop without turning quality assessment into a high-stakes test of fear. This design correction ensures that we protect data integrity while respecting the human limits of our frontline workforce.
However, we must examine what the leading standards authorities say about using external quality assessment as a direct measure of an individual’s skill. The United Kingdom Accreditation Service, or UKAS, released a position paper in 2017 stating clearly that external quality assessment is not a compulsory component of assessing individual competence. Instead, EQA is designed to guarantee the overall quality of the service being delivered, not to act as a personal test. In agreement with this view, the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, or CLSI, frames competence as a multi-element assessment. In their QMS03 guideline, they explain that true competency evaluation must combine direct observation, result reviews, blind specimens, and problem-solving exercises. Relying on a single test score is inadequate. (9,10)
The core of the trap lies in how we evaluate accuracy. When a monitoring system scores performance based on peer consensus, and the entire peer group begins to drift in the same direction, the accurate laboratory is suddenly the one that looks wrong. In this scenario, the person who reports truthfully becomes the outlier. Instead of being recognized for their precision, they are treated as an error that must be corrected. This is not a theoretical suspicion. Vietnam’s own published proficiency testing data across fifty-nine laboratories, published by Van and colleagues in 2023, shows a clear divergence. In their study of nine biochemical analytes across twelve samples, the expert group consensus actually diverged from the overall participant consensus on common analytes. This means that peer group divergence is a measured, documented phenomenon and not just a vague suspicion. It proves that peer groups can and do drift, and that the crowd is not always right. (9,11)
If we build a registry that punishes the outlier, we will receive uniform reports, but we will not receive true ones. Technicians are rational actors. If telling the truth exposes them to administrative correction or shame, they will simply adjust their numbers to match the consensus. This defeats the entire purpose of public health surveillance.
To avoid this, our proposed registry implements two critical design consequences. First, the record must be designed as an asset owned by the worker rather than an audit instrument held by the institution. Under a worker-owned model, honest recording builds your own professional capital and establishes your personal credibility. Under an institutional audit model, honest recording merely exposes you to punishment. Second, we must ensure that scoring references an objective laboratory method rather than a fluctuating crowd wherever it is possible. This anchors our evaluations in science rather than peer consensus.
During those years of processing diagnostic samples under constant pressure, I dreamed of a way to make our labor visible. But as I write this proposal, I must state a vital, hard boundary before anyone else points it out. It is worth being plain about what our proposed verified service record cannot do. A verified digital work history, no matter how securely recorded on a digital ledger, cannot substitute for formal professional licensure or national board certification.
The first gate is professional certification. The American Society for Clinical Pathology Board of Certification runs a domestic credential, MLS(ASCP), and an international one, MLS(ASCPi). The domestic credential has six eligibility routes and I checked them on the Board’s own page rather than trust a summary, because the summaries get this wrong. Route 1 wants a United States accredited laboratory programme. Route 2 wants an existing MLT(ASCP) credential, which a technician in Vinh Long does not have and cannot easily get. Route 3 was discontinued on the first of January 2023. What is actually open to a foreign-trained applicant is Route 5, and Route 5 does not start in the United States at all. It requires the international credential first, then a transcript evaluation verifying equivalency to a United States baccalaureate, then five years of full-time clinical experience within the last ten, across blood banking, chemistry, haematology, microbiology, immunology and urinalysis. (12)
That last clause is the argument of this book, stated by somebody else. The five years must be documented on the Board’s own Experience Documentation Form, signed by a laboratory director. The work has to have happened, and the only proof the Board will accept is a form filled in afterwards by a supervisor who has to remember it. A technician who did the work and whose director has retired, or whose institution has merged into another province, has no route at all. Not because she lacks the experience. Because she cannot produce the paper. (12,13)
The second gate is state licensing. About eleven states in the United States, including California and New York, license laboratory personnel separately from national certification. These states conduct their own audits, reviewing academic coursework hour by hour against their own rigid category lists. Because foreign transcripts are structured differently, they often fall short in a single chemistry or biology category. When this happens, the licensing board does not care about years of experience. The only accepted remedy is to go back to school and complete the missing coursework.
The third gate is the visa, which is completely independent and is almost always the hardest barrier to cross.
The honest conclusion is that our proposed digital record changes none of these rigid international rules. It does not waive a single coursework hour or bypass a visa interview. However, it does something that is worth far more than it first sounds. It makes the clinical experience route provable. To qualify for certification through experience, the board requires detailed proof of acceptable work in an accredited laboratory, verified directly by a laboratory director. Today, a technician from a provincial CDC in Vietnam has no credible way to prove their years of invisible labor to an international board. By providing a tamper-proof, verified history of their actual diagnostic contributions, we turn their silent service into a verifiable asset. It does not guarantee a visa, but it gives a hardworking technician a real fighting chance.
We must not make promises to our workforce that we cannot keep. This proposal does not offer a magic key to escape across borders. Instead, we must present this system for what it actually is: a tool to make the “N years of experience” route provable. It is a verified asset for postgraduate admissions, fellowship applications, and research roles where formal licenses are not required. By acknowledging these institutional barriers plainly, we protect our integrity and build a system that remains useful within its true boundaries.
To understand why this record matters, we must look at global migration. The data is sobering. A June 2021 report by Batalova and Fix from the Migration Policy Institute analyzed the American labor force. They found roughly eight million college-educated immigrants. But one in four of them, or two million people, is unemployed or working a job that only requires a high school education. This is brain waste. Those educated abroad are underemployed at a markedly higher rate of twenty-nine percent, compared to twenty-one percent for those educated domestically. English proficiency is the strongest predictor of this gap. But the lack of verifiable work history is a silent, massive barrier (6,9,14).
Our proposed record directly chips away at this barrier. It does not replace the exam. But it makes the existing experience route provable. The Board accepts clinical experience in place of an American laboratory programme, but only when it is attested on its own form by a laboratory director. Our secure, tamper-proof ledger provides that provable history. Beyond boards, the record carries weight in graduate admissions. Most admissions committees now use holistic reviews. In fact, roughly sixty percent of Master of Public Health programs no longer require standardized GRE tests. What a verified service history can do in such a file is narrower than I first wrote: it substantiates a claim the applicant is already making about their bench experience, rather than outranking transcripts or referees. I have no evidence about how admissions committees weigh an unaccredited foreign logbook, and I should not pretend otherwise. It opens doors. It provides undeniable proof of competence for fellowship applications and research roles that do not require state licenses.
Yet, we must be completely honest about our goals. Crossing an ocean is not the priority for most of our technicians. For them, the largest realistic market for recognition is inside Vietnam itself. We want to solve a domestic problem. By establishing a portable, verified record, we allow underrepresented local technicians to prove their worth. They can move across provincial boundaries. They can apply for national programs or seek donor-funded research roles. We do not promise an easy visa or a guaranteed salary bump. There is no trial evidence for those outcomes. We simply provide a verified asset. It lets our frontline workers own their own labor.
Here in Vietnam, our public health institutes have already delivered quality systems at scale. The commune-level quality assessment work described earlier is the proof that this reaches rural staff, not only provincial ones. However, I must state an important fact that we cannot afford to gloss over in this proposal. No per-technologist external quality assessment data exists publicly in Vietnam. Our national data is published entirely at the laboratory level, meaning we have no public record of how individual technicians perform on these tests.
There is an older way of allocating professional opportunity in any public service, and it is worth naming plainly rather than implying it. A training slot, a transfer, a place on a course: these have often moved through who knows whom, who spoke for you, whose department you came up in. Our proposed system of verified service records runs on something else entirely, namely what you did. Both approaches share the same ultimate objective, which is to prove that a worker is trustworthy and capable. However, one of these approaches allocates professional opportunities by connection, while the other allocates those exact same opportunities by verified evidence. In sociological terms, this is a shift from particularism to universalism. It shifts the entire workforce from a model of personal patronage to one of objective, standardized proof.
Despite these academic debates, the practical lesson for our healthcare system is clear. By building a verified digital record of service, we create an honest ladder for the unconnected. This proposal does not ask to change national civil service laws or demand new funding lines. It simply turns invisible daily labor into a portable, verified professional asset. It allows the quiet work done in provincial labs to speak for itself, bypassing the need for personal connections and ensuring that merit, not patronage, determines who rises.
I must state our limits honestly. There is currently no trial evidence or randomized controlled study evaluating how this decentralized, worker-owned model affects reporting accuracy or staff retention in low-resource provincial laboratories like ours in Vietnam. We are proposing a logical, evidence-informed framework to test these ideas. By giving our technicians ownership of their verified logs and anchoring their scores in objective methods, we can turn our registry into a safe ladder for professional growth rather than a dangerous trap.
